doc.title: Tom Lellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 31, 2007

chapter: Advice for singers and life on the road
title: Humility, hauling gear and the Fender Rhodes
summary: They discuss his lack of airs, carrying his own keyboard and amps, and the trouble of carrying a Fender Rhodes up six floors in New York.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: No, it’s good advice. And I did enjoy your performance last night and thought you had a good way with the audience.
And I think the musicians you work with appreciate the fact that — this is such a little thing — but when the gig is over like you’re in there helping load the car and all that stuff.
You know it’s just like such a way to be.

Yeah. I’m, that’s what I mean, I don’t think I’m superior to anyone or inferior, but certainly not superior. And I know those guys are so talented. And now I’m playing and I’m lugging around my own keyboard and guitar. So no, no airs, no airs.
Yeah. I wonder if you ever said boy why did I learn piano, now I’ve got to buy something, I’ve got to buy a PA, I’ve got to like —
Well I used to have to carry that around, as a singer you have to carry your own PA, but then it got much worse with heavy keyboards and Fender Rhodes —
Oh God, did you own one of those?

Oh I had a Fender Rhodes and I lived, when I first moved to New York I lived on the sixth floor of an elevator building and the elevator would break constantly and I would have to lug that thing up six floors. It was insane, yeah. And I remember a number of times I hit the landing and the thing went over, and it knocked all the screws out. It was so impacted, all the screws unscrewed and I had to go upstairs, get a screwdriver and put it back together before I put it in the car to go to the gig. Yeah. I’ve been there.

I always, I take it for granted when I’m from here, playing a gig, and I can time it. I can leave my house 45 minutes before I’m supposed to be somewhere and play, because I know how long it’s going to take me and I know the load in, but I always felt sorry for © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-
people in Manhattan who had to play a gig and park their car somewhere and load in and then go re-park their car. That must be a little hard.
Yeah. What we do for love.

Yeah. You learn to — I bought a little GK amplifier — we were talking — changed my life. I mean they made things smaller and more compact and you used to have to lug around big Fender Rhodes and big amps and it’s gotten a little better.
That is one good thing, the older we get the smaller our gear.
